title: dynamic-batch-penalty-scratchpad-mira
content:
Context:
- Quick personal log exploring the "dynamic batch penalty" phenomenon: when the runtime attempts to aggregate requests into a batch, small 1-2 request arrivals sometimes see worse tail latency because the system waits for a speculative extra token/req and then pays extra scheduling/context-switch cost. Trying to capture the effect under realistic traffic with mixed request sizes.

Goals:
- Measure incremental latency cost of waiting-for-batch vs immediate dispatch for small requests (seq len <= 128).
- Quantify break-even arrival rate where batching helps vs hurts.
- Sketch a simple heuristic to avoid backpressure for interactive, low-token requests.

Environment:
- Model: redwood-13b-8k (fp16, no quant) running on single A100-80G equivalent node in local dev cluster (dev-gpu-07).
- Serving binary: runtime-exec v1.9.2 (branch: dynamic-batch-probes).
- Worker config: max_batch_size=32, batch_wait_ms=8, concurrency_per_gpu=4.
- Input mix: 70% short chat (avg seq 60, stdev 20), 20% medium (seq 256), 10% long (seq 1024).
- Arrival process: Poisson baseline; intermittent microbursts simulated (10s bursts at +5x qps every 60s).

Experiment matrix (rough):
- Strategy A: baseline dynamic batching (batch_wait_ms=8)
- Strategy B: immediate dispatch for requests with expected tokens <= 96 (batch_wait_ms=0 for small)
- Strategy C: adaptive wait: start with wait=2ms for small requests, escalate to 8ms if steady queue forms
- Measures: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, mean throughput (inferred qps handled), GPU utilization, queue length distribution, batch size distribution, KV-cache hit-rate (prefix reuse)

Run notes and raw observations:
- Run 1 (Poisson qps=150):
  - A: p50=18ms, p95=72ms, p99=220ms; mean batch size=6.3; gpu util=44%
  - B: p50=14ms, p95=55ms, p99=140ms; mean batch size=3.1; gpu util=29%
  - C: p50=15ms, p95=60ms, p99=150ms; mean batch size=4.1; gpu util=34%
  - Notes: B improved tail by ~80ms at p99 vs A. But GPU utilization drops ~15pp — cost per token up.

- Run 2 (lower qps=60):
  - A: p50=22ms, p95=130ms, p99=420ms; mean batch size=2.0; gpu util=12%
  - B: p50=18ms, p95=95ms, p99=230ms; mean batch size=1.0; gpu util=8%
  - C: p50=19ms, p95=100ms, p99=260ms; mean batch size=1.3; gpu util=9.5%
  - Notes: At low qps, waiting for a larger batch (A) massively increases p99 because occasional delays accumulate. B still best for latency-sensitive small requests.

- Run 3 (bursty pattern avg=150 with 5x microbursts):
  - A: p50=19ms, p95=88ms, p99=310ms; mean batch size=7.8; gpu util=55% (during bursts spiked to 92%)
  - B: p50=15ms, p95=62ms, p99=180ms; mean batch size=2.9; gpu util=36%
  - C: p50=16ms, p95=68ms, p99=190ms; mean batch size=4.2; gpu util=42%
  - Notes: During bursts, batching wins for overall throughput (A higher gpu util) but still has worse p99 for the subset of single-token interactive requests. C trades off some tail for better util.

Batch size distribution comments:
- Baseline A shows heavy long tail in batch sizes: many small batches of 1-3 and occasional large batches 16-28 formed during bursts.
- B collapses to bimodal: mostly 1s and occasional >16 during bursts (because small requests bypass wait).

Simple per-request heuristic idea (sketch):
1) Estimate "small interactive" if expected_tokens <= 96 and request flagged as low-embargo (from clients).
2) If small interactive: do not wait if current queue depth < 2 OR estimated time-to-fill-to-3 < delta_t where delta_t = expected_remaining_tokens * token_process_ms (cheap approximation).
3) Allow short adaptive micro-wait (2-3ms) if there is a sustained inflow (exponential backoff for idle-to-busy transition).
4) Maintain metrics counter: tail_sensitivity_score per route (increase if p99 > SLO) and flip heuristics per-route.

Cost vs latency tradeoff (back-of-envelope):
- At qps=150, switching A->B reduced p99 by ~80ms but reduced token throughput/gpu util from 44%->29%: implies ~+40% unit cost per token (approx).
- For customer-facing interactive features, p99 improvement likely worth the cost up to a point; need to classify routes by latency-sensitivity.

Open questions / next steps:
- Repeat with quantized model and multi-GPU batching (how does cross-GPU scheduling affect penalty?).
- Collect per-route real production traces (sampled) to compute route-level break-even qps.
- Prototype the heuristic in runtime: feature-flagged rollout and A/B measure real cost delta.
- Explore combining with predicted KV-cache hit: if high prefix-hit predicted, prefer batching (amortizes context prep).
- Determine metric to decide threshold for immediate dispatch (simple: current queue time-to-fill-to-3 < 1ms).

Misc quick notes to self:
- When logging metrics for this test, include timestamped per-batch latency and whether each request was speculative-waited or immediate.
- Hook a trace-id from client to correlate user-perceived rtt with server p99 windows.
- Check PR #412 for batching loop changes (linked above).

TL;DR:
- Waiting a fixed 8ms to build larger batches helps throughput but can dramatically hurt p99 for low-qps interactive requests.
- A small adaptive micro-wait (2-3ms) or an immediate-dispatch opt-in for routes with expected small token counts gives most of the p99 improvement while retaining some batching benefits during bursts.
- Next: implement simple per-route opt-in + short adaptive waiter; run long 24h trace to quantify cost delta.
